fields.title: openPIP — Protein Interaction Portal
fields.faq:
Getting started

What is openPIP?

openPIP is an open-source web portal for hosting, searching and visualising protein-protein interaction (PPI) data. It is not itself a source of interactions: each deployment loads one or more published or in-house interaction datasets and makes them searchable, browsable, visualisable and downloadable. The datasets available on this site are listed on the Downloads page, with their provenance and citations on the About page.

Do I need an account?

No. Searching, browsing proteins, viewing networks, running enrichment, exporting your results and downloading whole datasets from the Downloads page all work without logging in. An account exists only for administering the site: loading datasets, editing this copy and managing files.

How do I run my first search? (tutorial)

A complete first search takes about a minute:

  1. On the home page, type a gene symbol into the search box, or click one of the example queries below it.
  2. Press Search. The results page opens with an interactive network: your query proteins and everything they interact with.
  3. Click a node to see that protein's identifiers, description and links to UniProt and other resources. Click an edge to see the evidence behind that interaction.
  4. Use Filter in the toolbar to drop low-confidence interactions or restrict the network to a single evidence category.
  5. Switch to the table and enrichment tabs below the network for a sortable list of interactions and functional enrichment of the result set.
  6. Use Download to export the network in the format your next tool expects.

What can I search with?

Gene symbols (TP53), UniProt accessions (P04637) and Ensembl identifiers all work. Separate multiple queries with commas or newlines to build a network around a whole gene list, for example TP53, MDM2, CDKN1A. The sidebar reports which of your queries were found and which were not.

My identifiers are in another format. What do I do?

Convert them first. UniProt ID mapping and DAVID Gene ID Conversion both translate most common identifier types into gene symbols or UniProt accessions.

Why did my search return nothing?

Usually one of three reasons: the identifier is misspelled or is an alias this portal does not index; the protein exists in the database but has no interactions in the loaded datasets; or the protein was never assayed in the underlying screens. Check the spelling in the protein browser, which lists every protein in the database and lets you search it directly, and try the UniProt accession instead of the gene symbol.

Working with results

How do I read the network?

Nodes are proteins and edges are interactions. Query proteins are drawn in a different colour from their interaction partners, and edge colours indicate the evidence category the interaction came from. The Legend button in the toolbar shows the exact colour scheme for this site, which the site administrator can change.

How do I see the evidence behind one interaction?

Click the edge. The panel that opens lists the individual experiments supporting that interaction: detection method, source dataset, publication and confidence score where the source dataset provides one.

Can I filter the results?

Yes, from the Filter menu in the toolbar. You can set a minimum confidence score, include or exclude individual evidence categories, and switch the filter mode between showing everything, only interactions between your query proteins, or only interactions between a query protein and a new interactor. Filters apply to the network, the tables and any export you make afterwards.

Can I change the layout or save a picture of the network?

The Layout menu offers force-directed (Cola and CoSE), concentric, circle and grid layouts; drag nodes to rearrange them by hand, scroll to zoom and drag the background to pan. To save the figure, choose Download and pick PNG or JPG, which exports the network exactly as it appears on screen.

What are the enrichment tabs?

They run functional enrichment on the proteins in your result set: Gene Ontology (molecular function, biological process, cellular component), Reactome and KEGG pathways, CORUM complexes, subcellular localisation, and tissue expression. Each table notes the external service and version the annotations came from, so results stay reproducible and citable.

Getting data out

Which export formats are available?

From the Download menu on a results page: SIF (simple interaction format), interactions as CSV, interactors as CSV, FASTA sequences, PSI-MI TAB 2.5, and PNG or JPG images of the network. No account is needed for any of them.

How do I get my results into Cytoscape?

Two ways. If Cytoscape Desktop is running on the same computer as your browser, use Open in Cytoscape and the network is sent straight across via CyREST, no files involved. Otherwise export the network as SIF (or CSV, if you want the interaction attributes) and import the file in Cytoscape through File > Import > Network from File.

How do I download a whole dataset instead of a search?

Go to the Downloads page, which lists every dataset hosted here with its release year and available formats. No account is needed.

Can I query openPIP from a script?

Yes, and no API key is needed. The API page documents four routes in: deep links you can paste into a paper or a wiki, a public CORS-enabled REST API with interactive docs, a typed Python SDK for notebooks and pipelines, and PSICQUIC support, so any tool already written against BioGRID, IntAct or STRING works against openPIP unchanged. The Documentation page covers the web interface in more depth.

Data, citation and contributing

Where does the interaction data come from?

From the datasets loaded into this instance, each of which is described, attributed and citable on the About page. openPIP does not generate or predict interactions, and it does not silently merge datasets: every interaction keeps the source it came from, which is why an edge can carry evidence from more than one dataset.

Why does a dataset here report a different number of interactions than its paper?

Identifiers are mapped to current gene and protein annotations at load time, and interactions that cannot be mapped to a protein-coding gene are not shown. Annotation models change between releases, so counts drift slightly from those published at the time. The dataset's own record on the About page is the authoritative description.

What does the confidence score mean, and why do some interactions not have one?

Confidence scores are supplied by the source dataset, not computed by openPIP, so their meaning is defined by that dataset's publication and they are only comparable within a dataset. Interactions from datasets that do not publish a score are shown without one; they are not lower quality, just unscored. Use a score threshold to rank and prioritise interactions, not to judge whether an interaction is real.

How do I cite openPIP and the data?

Cite the openPIP paper for the portal and cite each dataset you used separately. Both citations are given on the About page.

I found a bug, or I want a dataset added.

Get in touch through the Contact page. openPIP is open source (github.com/BaderLab/openPIP), so you can also run your own instance with your own data.
